HEAD & NECK__Applied / Clinical Anatomy:
Why this matters: the head & neck packs airway, vessels, nerves & glands into a tiny space — so the clinical anatomy is dense & high-yield: facial palsy, neck lumps, thyroid surgery, salivary stones, airway emergencies and head injury. This subtab ties it together into the scenarios you’ll be examined on.
Facial Nerve Palsy — UMN vs LMN
The key distinction
  • LMN lesion (Bell’s palsy, CN VII itself) → weakness of the WHOLE ipsilateral face, including the forehead
  • UMN lesion (stroke) → forehead SPARED (the upper face has bilateral cortical input)
CN VII beyond movement
  • Also carries taste (anterior ⅔ tongue via chorda tympani), supplies stapedius (→ hyperacusis) & drives lacrimation/salivation
  • Five branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical (“Two Zebras Bit My Coat”)
Neck Lumps & the Triangles
Midline lumps
  • Thyroglossal cyst — moves up on swallowing AND tongue protrusion (tethered to the foramen caecum); at/below the hyoid
  • Thyroid masses (goitre/nodule) move with swallowing but not tongue protrusion
Lateral lumps
  • Branchial cyst — anterior to the upper ⅓ of sternocleidomastoid (2nd branchial cleft remnant); young adults
  • Lymphadenopathy (infection/lymphoma/metastasis); Virchow’s node (left supraclavicular) = gastric cancer
  • Cystic hygroma, carotid body tumour (pulsatile, at the bifurcation)
Thyroid & Parathyroid Surgery
Nerves at risk
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve — in the tracheo-oesophageal groove near the inferior thyroid artery; injury → hoarse voice (vocal cord palsy); bilateral injury → airway obstruction
  • External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve — near the superior thyroid artery; injury → weak, tiring voice (can’t sing high — cricothyroid)
Parathyroids
  • Four glands behind the thyroid; inadvertent removal → hypocalcaemia (perioral tingling, Chvostek’s & Trousseau’s signs, tetany)
The Salivary Glands
Parotid
  • The facial nerve (CN VII) runs through it (dividing it into lobes) — a parotid tumour or surgery can cause facial palsy
  • Secretomotor supply is CN IX (glossopharyngeal, via the otic ganglion); its duct (Stensen’s) opens opposite the 2nd upper molar; mumps causes painful swelling
Submandibular
  • Drains via Wharton’s duct into the floor of the mouth; the commonest site of salivary stones (mixed, viscous saliva)
  • A stone → painful swelling at mealtimes
Airway Emergencies
Cricothyroidotomy
  • Emergency airway through the cricothyroid membrane (between the thyroid & cricoid cartilages) — a quick, superficial, relatively avascular route
Tracheostomy
  • A planned airway through the 2nd–4th tracheal rings (below the thyroid isthmus)
  • The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring — the landmark for cricoid pressure
The Scalp & Head Injury
The scalp (SCALP)
  • Skin · Connective tissue (dense, vascular) · Aponeurosis (epicranius) · Loose areolar tissue · Pericranium
  • Wounds bleed profusely (vessels held open by the dense connective tissue)
  • The loose areolar layer is the “dangerous area” — infection spreads here & can reach the cranial venous sinuses via emissary veins (→ meningitis)
Intracranial bleeds
  • Extradural — middle meningeal artery at the pterion (thin bone); a lucid interval then decline; lens (biconvex) shape
  • Subdural — torn bridging veins (elderly/alcoholics); crescent shape; slower
Ear, Eye & the Cavernous Sinus
Otitis media / mastoiditis — middle-ear infection can spread to the mastoid air cells; the facial nerve runs nearby.
Conductive vs sensorineural — Rinne & Weber tests localise the hearing loss.
CN III palsy — “down & out” eye, ptosis, fixed dilated pupil (a surgical CN III = aneurysm/uncal herniation).
Horner’s syndrome — ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis (sympathetic chain — Pancoast tumour, carotid dissection).
Cavernous sinus — carries CN III, IV, V1, V2 & VI + the internal carotid; thrombosis (facial infection via the ophthalmic veins) threatens them all.
Vessels & Lymphatics of the Neck
Common carotid bifurcates at ~C4 (upper border of the thyroid cartilage) into internal & external carotids.
Carotid sinus (baroreceptor, CN IX) & carotid body (chemoreceptor) sit at the bifurcation.
Internal jugular vein — the target for central venous access (lateral to the carotid).
Cervical lymph nodes (levels I–VI) — mapped for staging head & neck cancer; deep cervical nodes drain most of the region.
🧠 Mnemonics
Facial nerve branches — “Two Zebras Bit My Coat”: Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical.
Forehead spared = UMN; forehead involved = LMN (Bell’s palsy).
Scalp = SCALP: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar (dangerous), Pericranium.
Thyroglossal cyst moves on tongue protrusion; thyroid moves on swallowing only.
⭐ Exam Pearls
LMN (Bell’s) facial palsy involves the forehead; UMN (stroke) spares it.
Thyroglossal cyst rises on tongue protrusion & swallowing (foramen caecum tract).
Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (thyroid surgery) → hoarse voice; bilateral → airway obstruction.
External laryngeal nerve (near the superior thyroid artery) → weak/tiring voice.
Parathyroid damage → hypocalcaemia (Chvostek’s & Trousseau’s signs).
The facial nerve runs through the parotid; parotid pathology can cause facial palsy.
Submandibular gland (Wharton’s duct) is the commonest site of salivary stones.
Cricothyroidotomy = cricothyroid membrane; tracheostomy = 2nd–4th tracheal rings.
Extradural = middle meningeal artery at the pterion (lucid interval); subdural = bridging veins.
Cavernous sinus contains CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI + the internal carotid.
HEAD & NECK__Skull & Osteology:
Why this matters: the skull is a box of bones pierced by foramina that transmit every cranial nerve and vessel to the head. Learn the sutures & fontanelles, the three cranial fossae, the skull-base foramina and the mandible/TMJ, and base-of-skull fractures, cranial-nerve lesions and the fontanelle exam all make sense.
The Skull — Overview
Two functional parts
  • Neurocranium (8 bones) — encloses the brain: frontal, 2 parietal, 2 temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid
  • Viscerocranium (facial skeleton) — 14 bones: maxillae, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, palatine, inferior nasal conchae, vomer & the mandible
Calvaria & base
  • The calvaria (skull cap) is a “sandwich” of outer table, diploë (spongy bone with marrow & diploic veins) & inner table
  • The cranial base is stepped into three fossae
Sutures, Fontanelles & Landmarks
Sutures & points
  • Coronal (frontal–parietal), sagittal (between parietals), lambdoid (parietal–occipital), squamous
  • Bregma (coronal+sagittal), lambda (sagittal+lambdoid), pterion (frontal/parietal/temporal/sphenoid — thin, over the middle meningeal artery), asterion
Fontanelles
  • Anterior fontanelle (diamond, at the bregma) — closes at ~18 months; used to assess hydration (sunken) or ICP (bulging)
  • Posterior fontanelle (at the lambda) — closes at ~2–3 months
  • Craniosynostosis — premature suture fusion → an abnormal head shape
The Cranial Fossae
FossaBonesHolds / key features
AnteriorFrontal, ethmoid, sphenoid (lesser wing)Frontal lobes; cribriform plate (CN I)
MiddleSphenoid (greater wing), temporalTemporal lobes; the sella turcica / pituitary; most skull-base foramina
PosteriorOccipital, temporal (petrous)Brainstem & cerebellum; the foramen magnum
Foramina of the Skull Base
ForamenTransmits
Cribriform plateCN I (olfactory)
Optic canalCN II + ophthalmic artery
Superior orbital fissureCN III, IV, V1, VI + ophthalmic veins
Foramen rotundumCN V2 (maxillary)
Foramen ovaleCN V3 (mandibular) + accessory meningeal artery
Foramen spinosumMiddle meningeal artery (+ meningeal branch of V3)
Carotid canalInternal carotid artery
Internal acoustic meatusCN VII & VIII + labyrinthine artery
Jugular foramenCN IX, X, XI + internal jugular vein / sigmoid sinus
Hypoglossal canalCN XII
Stylomastoid foramenCN VII (exits the skull)
Foramen magnumMedulla/cord, vertebral arteries, CN XI (spinal root)
Standout facts. The superior orbital fissure carries the three ocular motor nerves (III, IV, VI) plus V1. Rotundum = V2, Ovale = V3. The jugular foramen carries the “middle” three (IX, X, XI); the hypoglossal canal = XII.
The Mandible & TMJ
Mandible
  • A body (with the tooth-bearing alveolar part) and two rami; each ramus has a condylar & a coronoid process, meeting at the angle
  • The mandibular foramen (inner ramus) admits the inferior alveolar nerve (dental block); the mental foramen transmits the mental nerve
Temporomandibular joint (TMJ)
  • A synovial joint with an articular disc; movements = elevation/depression, protrusion/retrusion & side-to-side
  • Depression begins with lateral pterygoid; anterior dislocation (wide yawn) locks the mouth open (condyle anterior to the articular tubercle)
The Orbit & Nasal Cavity
Orbit
  • A pyramidal cavity of seven bones (frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, maxilla, ethmoid, lacrimal, palatine)
  • Apex = optic canal; the superior & inferior orbital fissures transmit nerves/vessels
  • Blowout fracture — the thin floor (maxilla) fractures, trapping the inferior rectus (diplopia on upgaze); a medial-wall (ethmoid) blowout instead traps the medial rectus (horizontal diplopia)
Nasal cavity & sinuses
  • Divided by the septum; lateral wall has the superior, middle & inferior conchae
  • Paranasal sinuses — frontal, maxillary, ethmoidal & sphenoidal (air-filled, drain into the meatuses); the maxillary sinus drains “uphill” (sinusitis)
Clinical Correlations
Base-of-skull fracture — “raccoon eyes” (periorbital bruising), Battle’s sign (mastoid bruising), CSF rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea & haemotympanum.
Pterion fracture → torn middle meningeal artery → extradural haematoma.
Cribriform plate fracture → CSF rhinorrhoea & anosmia (CN I).
Anterior fontanelle — bulging = raised ICP/meningitis; sunken = dehydration.
Craniosynostosis — premature suture fusion (e.g. sagittal → scaphocephaly).
Le Fort fractures — classic midface fracture patterns (I–III).
🧠 Mnemonics
Superior orbital fissure — CN III, IV, V1, VI (the eye-movement nerves + V1).
Rotundum = V2; Ovale = V3 (“Standing Room Only”: Superior orbital fissure V1, Rotundum V2, Ovale V3).
Jugular foramen = 9, 10, 11 (glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory).
Anterior fontanelle closes ~18 months; posterior ~2–3 months.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Neurocranium = 8 bones; viscerocranium = 14; the pterion overlies the middle meningeal artery.
Anterior fossa = frontal lobes/CN I; middle = pituitary + most foramina; posterior = brainstem/cerebellum + foramen magnum.
Optic canal = CN II; superior orbital fissure = III, IV, V1, VI.
Foramen rotundum = V2; foramen ovale = V3; foramen spinosum = middle meningeal artery.
Internal acoustic meatus = CN VII & VIII; jugular foramen = IX, X, XI; hypoglossal canal = XII.
Facial nerve exits via the stylomastoid foramen.
Inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular foramen (dental block).
TMJ is synovial with a disc; anterior dislocation locks the jaw open.
Orbital blowout fracture traps inferior rectus → diplopia on upgaze.
Base-of-skull fracture: raccoon eyes, Battle’s sign, CSF rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea.
HEAD & NECK__Face, Scalp & Muscles of Fa:
Why this matters: the face is a sheet of small muscles (all CN VII) laid on the skin, with sensation from the trigeminal (CN V) and a scalp that bleeds famously. Learn the facial muscles & nerve, the trigeminal territories and the scalp layers/supply, and Bell’s palsy, facial lacerations and the danger triangle all make sense.
Muscles of Facial Expression
Key principles
  • Develop from the 2nd pharyngeal arch → all supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII)
  • Most insert into skin (not bone), so they move the skin; there is no investing deep fascia over them
  • Arranged as sphincters & dilators around the eye, nose & mouth
High-yield muscles
  • Orbicularis oculi — closes the eye (palpebral = blink, orbital = forced); loss → corneal exposure
  • Orbicularis oris — closes/purses the lips (speech, whistling)
  • Buccinator — compresses the cheek, keeps food on the teeth (CN VII, not a muscle of mastication); pierced by the parotid duct
  • Occipitofrontalis — raises the eyebrows (bellies joined by the galea aponeurotica)
  • Platysma — tenses the neck skin
The Facial Nerve (CN VII)
Course
  • Enters the internal acoustic meatus → runs in the facial canal (geniculate ganglion) → exits the stylomastoid foramen → through the parotid → 5 terminal branches
  • Intracranial branches: greater petrosal (→ lacrimal & nasal glands), nerve to stapedius, chorda tympani
Functions (mixed nerve)
  • Motor: muscles of facial expression + stapedius, posterior belly of digastric & stylohyoid
  • Special sensory (taste): anterior ⅔ of the tongue (via chorda tympani)
  • Parasympathetic: lacrimal, submandibular & sublingual glands
  • 5 branches: Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical (“Two Zebras Bit My Coat”)
Sensory Supply — the Trigeminal Nerve (CN V)
DivisionExitSensory territory
V1 (ophthalmic)Superior orbital fissureForehead, upper eyelid, dorsum of the nose, cornea
V2 (maxillary)Foramen rotundumLower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, side of the nose
V3 (mandibular)Foramen ovaleLower lip, chin, jaw (+ general sensation of the anterior ⅔ tongue)
The angle of the jaw is NOT trigeminal — it is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2–C3). So a “numb chin but normal jaw angle” still fits a V3 lesion. V3 also carries the motor supply to the muscles of mastication.
The Scalp — Layers, Blood & Nerve Supply
The five layers (SCALP)
  • Skin · dense Connective tissue (vessels & nerves) · Aponeurosis (galea/epicranius) · Loose areolar tissue (the “dangerous” layer) · Pericranium
  • The first three are bound together and move as a unit
Blood & nerve supply
  • Arteries (in the connective-tissue layer, richly anastomosing across the midline): from the ECA (superficial temporal, posterior auricular, occipital) & the ICA/ophthalmic (supratrochlear, supraorbital)
  • Nerves: anterior scalp — trigeminal (supratrochlear/supraorbital V1, zygomaticotemporal V2, auriculotemporal V3); posterior — cervical (greater occipital C2, lesser occipital C2–C3, third occipital C3)
Scalp wounds bleed profusely — the arteries are held open by the dense connective tissue & anastomose freely. The loose areolar layer lets infection/blood spread widely & reach the cranial venous sinuses via emissary veins.
Blood Supply of the Face
Arteries
  • The facial artery (from the ECA) crosses the inferior border of the mandible at the anterior edge of masseter (a palpable pulse), runs tortuously to the medial canthus as the angular artery
  • The superficial temporal artery (ECA terminal branch) & supraorbital/supratrochlear (from the ophthalmic) complete the supply — a rich anastomosis
Veins & the danger triangle
  • The facial vein is valveless and connects to the cavernous sinus (via the ophthalmic veins & the pterygoid plexus)
  • The “danger triangle” (nose to the corners of the mouth) — infection here can spread to cause cavernous sinus thrombosis
Clinical Correlations
Bell’s palsy — LMN CN VII palsy → the whole ipsilateral face incl. the forehead (± dry eye, hyperacusis, loss of taste, depending on level).
UMN facial lesion (stroke) — spares the forehead (bilateral cortical input to the upper face).
Corneal (blink) reflex — afferent V1, efferent VII; tests both nerves.
Trigeminal neuralgia — paroxysmal, severe V2/V3 pain triggered by touch/chewing.
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus — V1 shingles; Hutchinson’s sign (vesicles on the nose tip = nasociliary → risk to the eye).
Danger triangle infection — can seed the cavernous sinus (valveless facial vein).
🧠 Mnemonics
Facial nerve branches — “Two Zebras Bit My Coat”: Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical.
Muscles of facial expression = CN VII (2nd arch); muscles of mastication = CN V3 (1st arch).
Scalp = SCALP: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar, Pericranium.
Corneal reflex — V1 in, VII out.
⭐ Exam Pearls
All muscles of facial expression are supplied by CN VII (2nd pharyngeal arch).
Buccinator is CN VII (facial expression), not a muscle of mastication.
Facial nerve: internal acoustic meatus → facial canal → stylomastoid foramen → parotid → 5 branches.
CN VII also = taste (ant ⅔ tongue), stapedius, and lacrimal/submandibular/sublingual glands.
Facial sensation = trigeminal (V1 forehead, V2 cheek, V3 jaw); angle of jaw = great auricular (C2–3).
Scalp arteries anastomose freely (ECA + ophthalmic) → wounds bleed heavily.
Scalp nerves: anterior trigeminal, posterior cervical (occipital nerves).
Facial artery pulse is felt where it crosses the mandible at the anterior masseter.
Valveless facial vein connects the danger triangle to the cavernous sinus.
Bell’s palsy involves the forehead; a stroke spares it.
HEAD & NECK__Neck:
Why this matters: the neck is a crowded tube organised by fascial layers and mapped into triangles by sternocleidomastoid. Learn the fascia & spaces, the triangle contents, the cervical plexus and the carotid sheath, and central lines, neck dissections, the accessory nerve and deep-space infections all make sense.
Cervical Fascia & Spaces
Deep cervical fascia — 4 layers
  • Investing — surrounds the whole neck; splits to enclose SCM & trapezius (and the parotid/submandibular glands)
  • Pretracheal — encloses the thyroid, trachea & oesophagus (+ the strap muscles)
  • Prevertebral — wraps the vertebral column & deep muscles; extends as the axillary sheath
  • Carotid sheath — the common/internal carotid, IJV & vagus
Why spaces matter
  • The fascial planes create potential spaces (retropharyngeal, “danger” space) that channel infection down into the mediastinum
  • Superficial fascia contains platysma
The Triangles of the Neck
Anterior triangle
  • Bounded by the midline, the mandible & the anterior border of SCM
  • Subdivided into the submental, submandibular (digastric), carotid & muscular triangles
  • Contains the carotid sheath, larynx/thyroid, strap muscles & submandibular gland
Posterior triangle
  • Bounded by the posterior border of SCM, the anterior border of trapezius & the clavicle
  • Contents: the accessory nerve (CN XI), the cervical plexus branches (at Erb’s point), the brachial plexus trunks & the 3rd part of the subclavian artery, EJV & the inferior belly of omohyoid
The accessory nerve is superficial in the posterior triangle (only under investing fascia) — vulnerable in lymph-node biopsy; injury weakens trapezius (drooping shoulder).
Sternocleidomastoid & the Strap Muscles
Sternocleidomastoid (SCM)
  • Sternal & clavicular heads → the mastoid process & superior nuchal line
  • Supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI) (+ C2–3 proprioception)
  • Unilateral: tilts the head to the same side & rotates the face to the opposite side; bilateral: flexes the neck; congenital torticollis
Strap (hyoid) muscles
  • Infrahyoid (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) depress the hyoid/larynx — mostly the ansa cervicalis (C1–C3); thyrohyoid is C1 alone
  • Suprahyoid (digastric, stylohyoid, mylohyoid, geniohyoid) elevate the hyoid
The Cervical Plexus
Formation & cutaneous branches
  • From the anterior rami of C1–C4, deep to SCM
  • Cutaneous branches emerge at the nerve point (Erb’s point) — the middle of the posterior SCM border: lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical & supraclavicular nerves
Motor branches
  • Ansa cervicalis (C1–C3) — the infrahyoid strap muscles
  • Phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) — the sole motor supply to the diaphragm (“C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive”)
The Carotid Sheath & Root of the Neck
Carotid sheath
  • Contains the common/internal carotid artery (medial), internal jugular vein (lateral) & the vagus nerve (posterior, between them)
  • The common carotid bifurcates at ~C4; the carotid sinus (baroreceptor) & body (chemoreceptor) sit here
Root of the neck
  • The subclavian artery arches over the 1st rib in 3 parts (relative to scalenus anterior); the brachial plexus & artery pass through the interscalene triangle
  • The thoracic duct arches over on the left to drain into the left venous angle; the cervical pleura rises above the 1st rib
Clinical Correlations
Accessory nerve injury (posterior triangle biopsy) → trapezius weakness & a drooping shoulder.
Central venous access — the internal jugular vein (in the carotid sheath, lateral to the carotid).
Neck dissection (levels I–VI) maps the cervical nodes for head & neck cancer staging.
Ludwig’s angina — cellulitis of the submandibular/floor-of-mouth space; can obstruct the airway.
Retropharyngeal abscess — infection tracks down the fascial “danger space” into the mediastinum.
Thoracic outlet syndrome — a cervical rib/scalene compresses the lower plexus & subclavian vessels in the interscalene triangle.
🧠 Mnemonics
Cervical plexus cutaneous branches — “GLoTS”: Great auricular, Lesser occipital, Transverse cervical, Supraclavicular.
Phrenic = C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive.
Carotid sheath — carotid medial, IJV lateral, Vagus in between/behind (“VAN” posteriorly).
SCM — tilts to the same side, turns the face to the opposite side.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Deep cervical fascia: investing, pretracheal, prevertebral, carotid sheath.
SCM divides the neck into anterior & posterior triangles.
Posterior triangle: accessory nerve (superficial), cervical & brachial plexuses, 3rd part of subclavian artery.
Accessory nerve injury in the posterior triangle → drooping shoulder.
Ansa cervicalis (C1–3) supplies the strap muscles except thyrohyoid (C1 alone).
Cervical plexus branches emerge at Erb’s point (mid-posterior SCM border).
Phrenic nerve = C3–C5, on scalenus anterior.
Carotid sheath: carotid, internal jugular vein & vagus nerve.
The thoracic duct drains to the left venous angle at the root of the neck.
Deep-neck-space infections can spread to the mediastinum.
HEAD & NECK__Special Regions:
Why this matters: the head’s “special regions” — the tongue, pharynx, larynx, ear & orbit — are cranial-nerve-dense and exam-favourite. Learn the tongue & laryngeal innervation, the pharyngeal muscles, the ear’s three parts and the extraocular muscles, and hypoglossal palsy, hoarseness, otitis media and the eye-movement nerves all make sense.
The Tongue
Muscles
  • Extrinsic (position): Genioglossus (protrudes), Hyoglossus (depresses), Styloglossus (retracts/elevates), Palatoglossus (elevates the back)
  • All are CN XII (hypoglossal) — EXCEPT palatoglossus (CN X, vagus)
Sensation (a classic split)
  • Anterior ⅔: general = lingual nerve (V3); taste = chorda tympani (VII)
  • Posterior ⅓: general & taste = glossopharyngeal (IX)
  • The epiglottis/valleculae: vagus (X) (internal laryngeal)
Hypoglossal (XII) palsy. On protrusion the tongue deviates TOWARD the side of the lesion (the weak genioglossus can’t push that side forward) — “the tongue points to the lesion.”
The Pharynx
Structure
  • Three parts: nasopharynx, oropharynx & laryngopharynx
  • Muscular wall: 3 circular constrictors (superior, middle, inferior) + 3 longitudinal (stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus)
Innervation & Waldeyer’s ring
  • Motor: pharyngeal plexus (CN X) for all EXCEPT stylopharyngeus (CN IX); sensory mainly CN IX
  • Waldeyer’s ring — the pharyngeal (adenoid), tubal, palatine & lingual tonsils
Pharyngeal pouch (Zenker’s). A mucosal herniation through Killian’s dehiscence (a weak area between the thyropharyngeus & cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor) → dysphagia, regurgitation & halitosis.
The Larynx
Cartilages & cords
  • Thyroid, cricoid (the only complete ring), paired arytenoids & the epiglottis
  • The vocal folds bound the rima glottidis (the narrowest part of the adult airway)
Muscles & nerves
  • All intrinsic muscles = recurrent laryngeal nerve, EXCEPT cricothyroid (external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve — tenses the cords)
  • The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only ABDUCTOR (“opens” the cords) — vital for breathing
  • Sensation: above the cords = internal laryngeal nerve; below = recurrent laryngeal nerve
The Ear
PartContainsNote
ExternalAuricle, external acoustic meatus, tympanic membraneCollects & conducts sound
MiddleMalleus, incus, stapes; the Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube; stapediusAmplifies; tube equalises pressure to the nasopharynx
InnerCochlea (hearing) & vestibular apparatus (balance); CN VIIITransduction of sound & balance
Otitis media is common in children — the Eustachian tube is shorter, wider & more horizontal, so nasopharyngeal infection ascends easily. Conductive loss (external/middle ear) vs sensorineural loss (cochlea/CN VIII) is separated by the Rinne & Weber tests.
The Orbit & Eye
Extraocular muscles & nerves
  • Four recti (superior, inferior, medial, lateral) + two obliques (superior, inferior)
  • “LR6 SO4, rest 3”: Lateral Rectus = CN VI, Superior Oblique = CN IV, all others = CN III
Reflexes & palsies
  • Pupillary light reflex: afferent CN II, efferent CN III (parasympathetic)
  • CN III palsy — “down & out” eye, ptosis, dilated pupil; CN IV — vertical diplopia (going downstairs); CN VI — failure to abduct (horizontal diplopia)
Clinical Correlations
Hypoglossal palsy — tongue deviates toward the lesion on protrusion.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy — hoarseness; bilateral → airway obstruction (posterior cricoarytenoids paralysed).
Pharyngeal pouch — dysphagia & regurgitation via Killian’s dehiscence.
Glue ear / acute otitis media — conductive loss; the child’s Eustachian tube predisposes.
Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) — a complication of tonsillitis; the tonsil’s blood supply is chiefly the tonsillar branch of the facial artery.
Squint/diplopia — localise by the failing eye movement (LR6 SO4 rest 3).
🧠 Mnemonics
Tongue muscles — all “-glossus” are CN XII except palatoglossus (X).
Tongue points to the lesion (XII palsy).
Larynx — all intrinsics = recurrent laryngeal EXCEPT cricothyroid (external laryngeal); Posterior Cricoarytenoid = the only abductor (opens).
Eye muscles — “LR6 SO4, rest 3”.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Tongue: motor = CN XII (palatoglossus = X); ant ⅔ taste = VII, general = V3; post ⅓ = IX.
XII palsy → tongue deviates toward the lesion.
Pharynx: all muscles CN X except stylopharyngeus (CN IX).
Pharyngeal pouch herniates through Killian’s dehiscence.
All intrinsic laryngeal muscles = recurrent laryngeal, except cricothyroid (external laryngeal).
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal cords.
Above the cords sensation = internal laryngeal; below = recurrent laryngeal.
Ossicles: malleus, incus, stapes; Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx.
Extraocular nerves: LR6 (abducens), SO4 (trochlear), rest III (oculomotor).
Light reflex: afferent CN II, efferent CN III.
HEAD & NECK__Cranial Nerves I–XII:
Why this matters: the twelve cranial nerves are the exam’s favourite localiser — each has a function, a skull exit & a brainstem nucleus. Learn the master table, the parasympathetic four (III, VII, IX, X), the reflexes and the classic palsies, and every “which nerve?” question falls into place.

Names — “On Old Olympus’ Towering Tops A Finn And German Viewed Some Hops.” Type (S/M/B) — “Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most” (S,S,M,M,B,M,B,S,B,B,M,M).
Brainstem Levels & the Parasympathetic Four
Nuclei by level
  • Midbrain: III, IV
  • Pons: V, VI, VII, VIII
  • Medulla: IX, X, XII (+ the cranial part of XI)
  • The spinal accessory arises from the upper cervical cord (C1–C5)
Parasympathetic outflow (CN 3, 7, 9, 10)
  • III → ciliary ganglion (pupillary constrictor & ciliary muscle)
  • VII → pterygopalatine (lacrimal/nasal) & submandibular ganglia (submandibular/sublingual glands)
  • IX → otic ganglion (parotid)
  • X → the thoracic & abdominal viscera (to the distal ⅓ transverse colon)
The Ocular Motor Nerves (III, IV, VI)
Key facts
  • “LR6 SO4, rest 3” — lateral rectus = VI, superior oblique = IV, the rest = III
  • IV is the only nerve to exit the dorsal brainstem & it decussates (supplies the contralateral SO); it is the thinnest
  • VI has a long intracranial course with a sharp bend over the petrous apex (Dorello’s canal), so it is stretched in raised ICP — a false-localising sign
Palsies
  • III — “down & out” eye, ptosis, dilated pupil (surgical III = aneurysm/uncal herniation)
  • IV — vertical diplopia (worse looking down & in), head tilt away
  • VI — failure to abduct → horizontal diplopia
Trigeminal (V) & Facial (VII)
Trigeminal (V)
  • Sensation to the face in three divisions (V1 SOF, V2 rotundum, V3 ovale); V3 is motor to the muscles of mastication
  • The corneal reflex afferent (V1) & the jaw-jerk (V both)
Facial (VII)
  • Motor to facial expression + stapedius; taste ant ⅔ (chorda tympani); lacrimal/salivary glands
  • LMN (Bell’s) palsy — whole face incl. forehead; UMN spares the forehead
The Lower Cranial Nerves (IX, X, XI, XII)
IX, X, XI
  • IX — gag reflex afferent, carotid sinus/body, parotid, stylopharyngeus
  • X — gag reflex efferent, palate/larynx; a lesion → the uvula deviates AWAY from the lesion & hoarseness
  • XI — SCM & trapezius; injury → drooping shoulder
XII
  • Motor to the tongue; a lesion → the tongue deviates TOWARD the lesion on protrusion (“points to the lesion”)
Deviation rules. Tongue (XII) points toward the lesion; the uvula/palate (X) is pulled away from the lesion (toward the normal side).

Clinical Correlations
Cavernous sinus syndrome — affects CN III, IV, V1, V2 & VI (+ the internal carotid).
Jugular foramen (Vernet’s) syndrome — CN IX, X & XI.
Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) — CN VIII at the cerebellopontine angle (± V & VII).
Bell’s palsy — LMN CN VII, whole hemiface.
Bulbar palsy — LMN lesions of IX, X, XII → dysphagia, dysarthria, a wasted/fasciculating tongue.
Anosmia — CN I damage (cribriform-plate fracture, frontal lobe tumour).
🧠 Mnemonics
Names — On Old Olympus’ Towering Tops A Finn And German Viewed Some Hops.
Type — Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most (S/M/B).
Parasympathetic CNs — 3, 7, 9, 10 (ciliary, pterygopalatine/submandibular, otic, vagal).
Deviation — Tongue toward, uvula away (from the lesion).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Sensory-only CNs: I, II, VIII; the rest are motor or mixed.
Parasympathetic CNs: III, VII, IX, X (ciliary, pterygopalatine/submandibular, otic, vagal ganglia).
CN IV is the only nerve exiting the dorsal brainstem & decussates; CN VI bends over the petrous apex (a false-localising sign in raised ICP).
LR6 SO4, rest 3 (eye muscle nerves).
Corneal reflex: V1 in, VII out; gag reflex: IX in, X out; light reflex: II in, III out.
Jugular foramen transmits IX, X, XI; internal acoustic meatus VII & VIII.
Cavernous sinus contains III, IV, V1, V2, VI + internal carotid.
Tongue (XII) deviates toward the lesion; uvula (X) deviates away.
Bell’s palsy (LMN VII) involves the forehead; a stroke spares it.
Acoustic neuroma = CN VIII at the cerebellopontine angle.
HEAD & NECK__Vessels & Lymphatics:
Why this matters: the head & neck is fed by the carotid & vertebral arteries, drained by the jugular veins, and filtered by the cervical lymph nodes. Learn the external-carotid branches, the internal-carotid/vertebral circulation, the jugular veins and the node levels, and carotid disease, central lines and cancer staging all make sense.
The Carotid System
Common carotid
  • The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk; the left directly from the aortic arch
  • Ascends in the carotid sheath & bifurcates at ~C4 (upper thyroid cartilage) into the internal & external carotid
  • The carotid sinus (baroreceptor, CN IX) & carotid body (chemoreceptor) lie at the bifurcation
Internal carotid
  • NO branches in the neck; enters the carotid canal → the cavernous sinus
  • Gives the ophthalmic artery, then ends as the anterior & middle cerebral arteries (the anterior circulation of the circle of Willis)
The External Carotid Artery — 8 Branches
BranchSupplies
Superior thyroidThyroid, larynx
Ascending pharyngealPharynx, meninges
LingualTongue
FacialFace (crosses the mandible; tonsillar branch to the palatine tonsil)
OccipitalPosterior scalp
Posterior auricularBehind the ear
Maxillary (terminal)Deep face; gives the middle meningeal artery
Superficial temporal (terminal)Scalp; palpable temporal pulse (temporal arteritis)
“Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students” — Superior thyroid, Ascending pharyngeal, Lingual, Facial, Occipital, Posterior auricular, Maxillary, Superficial temporal. The maxillary & superficial temporal are the two terminal branches.
Vertebral & Subclavian Arteries
Vertebral artery
  • A branch of the subclavian; ascends the foramina transversaria (C6→C1), crosses the suboccipital triangle & foramen magnum
  • The two unite as the basilar artery → the posterior circulation of the brain
Subclavian branches
  • Vertebral, internal thoracic, thyrocervical trunk (1st part), costocervical trunk (2nd), dorsal scapular (3rd)
Circle of Willis. The two internal carotids (anterior) & the basilar (posterior, from the vertebrals) anastomose via the anterior & posterior communicating arteries — a collateral ring at the brain base.
Venous Drainage
Internal jugular vein (IJV)
  • The continuation of the sigmoid sinus, exiting the jugular foramen; runs in the carotid sheath
  • Receives the facial, lingual, pharyngeal & superior/middle thyroid veins; joins the subclavian → the brachiocephalic vein
  • Used for central venous access & the JVP
External jugular & danger triangle
  • The external jugular vein (posterior auricular + the posterior division of the retromandibular vein) crosses SCM superficially → the subclavian
  • The facial vein is valveless & connects to the cavernous sinus (danger-triangle infection)
Lymphatic Drainage
The node groups
  • A superficial ring (submental, submandibular, parotid, mastoid, occipital) drains the face/scalp
  • All lymph funnels into the deep cervical chain along the IJV, then the jugular lymph trunk
  • Key nodes: the jugulodigastric (tonsillar) node & the jugulo-omohyoid (tongue) node
Levels & terminal drainage
  • Surgically mapped as levels I–VI (I submental/submandibular, II–IV upper/mid/lower deep cervical, V posterior triangle, VI anterior/central)
  • Drains to the thoracic duct (left) or the right lymphatic duct (right) at the root of the neck
Clinical Correlations
Carotid atherosclerosis — a bruit at the bifurcation; a source of TIA/stroke; treated by carotid endarterectomy.
Temporal arteritis (GCA) — a tender, pulseless superficial temporal artery; risk of blindness → urgent steroids.
Virchow’s node (Troisier’s sign) — an enlarged left supraclavicular node from gastric cancer (via the thoracic duct).
Jugulodigastric node enlarges in tonsillitis/pharyngitis (the “tonsillar node”).
IJV cannulation — lateral to the carotid; raised, non-pulsatile JVP in right-heart failure.
Neck node level guides the search for a head & neck primary cancer.
🧠 Mnemonics
ECA branches — “Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students”: Superior thyroid, Ascending pharyngeal, Lingual, Facial, Occipital, Posterior auricular, Maxillary, Superficial temporal.
ICA has no branches in the neck (external carotid does the work there).
Two terminal ECA branches — Maxillary & Superficial temporal.
Virchow’s = left supraclavicular (thoracic duct drains here).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Right common carotid from the brachiocephalic; left directly from the aortic arch.
Common carotid bifurcates at C4; the internal carotid has no cervical branches.
ECA has 8 branches (SALFOPMS); the terminal two are maxillary & superficial temporal.
The maxillary artery gives the middle meningeal artery (extradural haematoma).
Vertebral artery ascends C6→C1 & forms the basilar (posterior circulation).
IJV = continuation of the sigmoid sinus via the jugular foramen; central-line target.
All head & neck lymph drains via the deep cervical chain (along the IJV).
Jugulodigastric = tonsillar node; jugulo-omohyoid = tongue node.
Cervical nodes are mapped as levels I–VI for cancer staging.
Temporal arteritis affects the superficial temporal artery — steroids urgently.
